Figure 1:Two paradigms for evaluating cybersecurity agents.Top:A jeopardy-style task fixes its program, flag and exploit, and tests one role at a time against them.Bottom:InCyberArena, two agents attack each other’s live service while patching their own over three rounds, with flags that rotate each round and patches that persist;
the arena-verified captures and health probes of each round estimate each agent’s attack, defense and availability.

Figure 2:Agentic challenge curation.(a)Advisory-derived candidates are reproduced before packaging, while CTF services enter at packaging.
Each challenge is verified and checked by three reviewer agents and a judge, and is returned for revision for up to four review rounds before admission.(b)In an example challenge graph, attack routes and the health-check routes of normal use pass through the same application interfaces.
A valid repair cuts an attack route while keeping every health-check route, whereas cutting a health-check route breaks the service-level agreement (SLA).

Figure 3:Campaign coverage and pairings.(a) Valid games per entrant and batch, with totals.
Gemini 3.7 Flash entered after batch 15 and Claude Opus 5 after batch 18, each at the shared prior.
(b) Record of the row entrant against the column entrant, where the higher game score wins and a tie counts as half a win (AppendixD.4).
Numbers count valid games.

Figure 4:(a) Posterior mean expected scores of the 12 agents, fitted from 466 valid games and averaged uniformly over the other entrants and 40 reference challenges (0–100%), with model-conditional 5–95% credible intervals.
(b) Fitted attack ability plotted against defense ability, in logits relative to the field.
The dashed diagonal marks parity, and the defense axis skips 0.3–0.78, where no agent lies.

Figure 5:Campaign progress.After every batch, the model is refit from the original prior and each entrant’s expected score is recomputed.
Each series begins with the entrant’s first valid game.
The horizontal axis counts cumulative valid campaign games.
Table2gives the final intervals.
Gemini 3.7 Flash and Claude Opus 5 join the campaign at later batches.

Figure 6:Six-axis profiles.Fitted attack and defense abilities on each of the six mechanism axes, in logits, combine each agent’s general ability with its specialty on that axis.
Axes: A access control, X input and execution, F files and resources, C cryptography and randomness, R parsing, S protocol and state.
Attack is shown in red with fill, defense in teal with a dashed line, and the dotted ring marks zero.

Figure 7:Observed capture, retention, and health-probe rates.Empirical percentages of rounds in which an entrant captured the opponent’s flag (attack) or kept its own (defense), and of health probes its service passed, pooled across all three rounds of its valid games without fitting the ability model.

Figure 8:Round-1 time to (a) the first accepted capture and (b) the first patch deployment, in the 466 games of batches 1–22, with one dot per game in which the named entrant had the event and a bar marking the median.

Figure 9:The six most frequent agent-error patterns for twelve agents in the 466 audited games.
Each cell is the percentage of an agent’s reviewed games with at least one such finding attributed to that agent.
Patterns overlap, and these are recorded findings, not failure rates per action.
Grok 4.6’s sparse action records make its low values hard to interpret.

Figure 10:Game trajectories of four case studies.Chronological event timelines for four games from Table4, showing attacker actions on the left rail (red swords, filled for captures and hollow otherwise) and defender actions on the right rail (teal shields and magnifying glass) across three rounds.
The cases illustrate four behaviors: a recorded exploit replay failing after a patch, routing around a blocked endpoint, sniffing network traffic to catch stolen credentials, and a persistent backdoor surviving a deployed entry-route patch.

Figure 11:Solo and contest capture rates.
(a) Solo, over all 40 reference challenges, counting capture in either of two single-round attempts as success.
(b) Solo and per-round contest rates on the 30 challenges solved solo by all three models, with 95% bootstrap intervals that resample challenges for solo and games for contest.

Figure 11:Solo and contest capture rates.
(a) Solo, over all 40 reference challenges, counting capture in either of two single-round attempts as success.
(b) Solo and per-round contest rates on the 30 challenges solved solo by all three models, with 95% bootstrap intervals that resample challenges for solo and games for contest.

Figure 12:Calls to the tool gatewayby tool, over the valid games.
Across the 466 valid games, agents made 53,511 calls to the game tools, averaging 115 per game.
Server-event counts are exact, while calls to the four tools without event records are counted from transcripts and undercounted.

Figure 14:The challenge interface.(a)Challenges specify deployment, attack objectives, functionality checks, and the agent briefing.(b)Arena calls cover one-time setup, objective placement, concurrent attack and defense, and end-of-round objective checks.(c)Read, execute, and write objectives share a plant-and-retrieve interface but require different evidence of success.(d)Verification facilities operate outside the defender-controlled service container.
Write verification reads permitted state through the host container API without executing code inside the service container.
